questions.q: What specific question does an implementation roadmap answer, per this lesson?
options: In what order does the build actually happen, and what has to finish before what else can start
Which stakeholders are happiest with the design
How much the entire project will cost in total
Which Salesforce edition LTV Global should purchase
questions.explain: A roadmap is fundamentally about sequencing and dependency — what must exist before something else can be built — not a cost estimate or a stakeholder satisfaction summary.

questions.q: Why doesn't the roadmap simply follow the same order this course taught its chapters in?
options: Because the course's chapter order was randomly assigned
Because Salesforce requires roadmaps to follow a fixed universal template
Because teaching order served pedagogical purposes, while build order has to follow actual dependencies — foundational work has to exist before business-unit features can be built on top of it
Because the course's chapter order is identical to the roadmap by design
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes teaching order (chosen for pedagogy) from build order (driven by genuine technical dependency), which is why the roadmap phases don't mirror the course's chapter sequence exactly.

questions.q: Why is Parts & Aftermarket's rollout (Phase 3) deliberately sequenced after Phase 2, rather than first, despite its stakeholder being the most performance-sensitive?
options: Because Parts & Aftermarket is considered the least important business unit
Because the integration hub and LDV strategy need to be proven against real production traffic from a lower-risk business unit before carrying the highest-volume unit's load
Because Parts & Aftermarket has no dependencies on any other phase
Because the Parts & Aftermarket VP requested to go last
questions.explain: The sequencing is driven by dependency and risk management, not priority — proving the integration hub and LDV strategy against a lower-risk BU first makes the eventual highest-volume rollout safer, not a sign Parts & Aftermarket matters less.

questions.q: How does Lesson 20's migration wave strategy relate to this lesson's implementation roadmap?
options: The migration waves run as a completely separate, unrelated project
The migration waves must all occur before Phase 0 begins
The migration waves replace the need for an implementation roadmap entirely
The migration waves are embedded inside the roadmap, each occurring at the phase where its prerequisite platform capability is actually ready
questions.explain: Each migration wave slots into the roadmap at the point where its prerequisite (such as Service Cloud existing before EMEA's EuroCRM data can be migrated) is actually satisfied, rather than running as an independent parallel track.

questions.q: What does this lesson say would happen with a roadmap sequenced by 'whoever is loudest goes first' instead of genuine dependency?
options: It would produce fragile sequencing that a Chapter 6 board member would catch immediately
It would be the most efficient possible roadmap
It would have no effect on the roadmap's quality
It would eliminate the need for Phase 0 foundational work
questions.explain: The lesson warns that priority-driven (rather than dependency-driven) sequencing produces a fragile roadmap, exactly the kind of flaw an Architecture Review Board would be expected to catch.
